title: Logarithmic fully dynamic planar nearest neighbors
formal: Does a uniform Las Vegas data structure maintain a finite set of planar points under insertions and deletions, answer exact Euclidean nearest-neighbor queries in \(O(\log(n+2))\) worst-case time, and support updates in expected amortized \(O(\log(n+2))\) time, using \(O((n+1)\log^c(n+2))\) space for some fixed constant \(c\)?
why: A logarithmic fully dynamic structure would establish the natural two-dimensional counterpart of a basic ordered-search interface.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. The 2025 incremental theorem has optimal logarithmic queries but a growing insertion overhead and no general deletion interface. A bounded later-work search did not locate a result meeting this explicit fully dynamic Las Vegas variant. Approximate high-dimensional indexing results do not meet its exact planar model; source proofs were not independently verified.

progress.text: Iacono–Nekrich give \(O(\log n)\) queries and \(O(\log^{1+\eta}n)\) insertions for fixed \(\eta>0\) in an incremental structure.

definitions: The structure initializes the empty set in constant time and space. An insertion supplies a real point not currently present and returns a stable handle. A deletion supplies the handle of a present point. A query supplies \(q\in\mathbb R^2\) and returns any present \(p\) minimizing \((p_x-q_x)^2+(p_y-q_y)^2\), or an empty marker. Ties may be resolved arbitrarily but correctly. At any instant \(n\) is the number of stored points. Use an algebraic real RAM with exact real addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero real, and comparisons, each at unit cost. A point coordinate, scalar, pointer or fixed-size record field occupies one cell. Reading, writing and following pointers cost one step; no floor, bit extraction from reals, or packing unbounded discrete information into a real is an available operation. The program is uniform and finite; there is no advice or free table construction. Each independently generated fair random bit costs one operation; sampling an arbitrary exact real number is not a primitive. All answers are exact on every terminating execution and the structure terminates almost surely. For every fixed finite legal operation sequence chosen independently of its random bits, with \(u\) updates and maximum set size \(M\), the expected total update time is \(O(u\log(M+2))\); each query separately has worst-case \(O(\log(n+2))\) time on every execution. Space holds on every execution, including retained points and temporary work. All constants are universal. This states the amortization convention using the maximum size of the sequence, without an adaptive-adversary guarantee. The space exponent \(c\) may be any fixed nonnegative integer. All logarithms are base two. The sequence and its real coordinates may depend on the program but are fixed before its random bits are sampled; the bounds impose no adaptive-adversary guarantee.

context_blocks.text: A nearest-neighbor query asks for an actual stored point minimizing Euclidean distance to the query. On a line, ordered search can inspect the predecessor and successor. In the plane, closeness depends on two coordinates together, and a nearby point in one coordinate can be far away in the other.

Deletion is a substantive operation. Removing the previously closest point can expose a different answer at many query locations, while the data structure must still answer whichever query arrives next. The target retains every allowed insertion and deletion sequence instead of assuming that the stored point set only grows.

The 2025 incremental result achieves \(O(\log n)\) queries and \(O(\log^{1+\eta}n)\) insertion time for fixed positive \(\eta\). Its query bound meets this target, but its insertion bound still has a growing factor over logarithmic time and the incremental interface does not include arbitrary deletions.

Randomness is permitted to affect work, not geometric correctness: every returned point must really minimize the squared distance, with any exact minimizer acceptable in a tie. Updates are bounded in expected total time over each fixed sequence, whereas a query must meet its time bound on every execution. These are separate promises.

The original source asks for logarithmic costs in the fully dynamic planar problem. The retained benchmark states an explicit Las Vegas variant with expected amortized updates, worst-case queries and near-linear space. Its real-arithmetic cost model does not claim a logarithmic bit complexity for arbitrary real coordinates.

Approximate-neighbor libraries, empirical query throughput and high-dimensional vector indexes address related applications but do not imply this exact two-dimensional worst-case interface. The space guarantee also counts temporary work and must hold for the current number of points.

answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a single uniform Las Vegas representation and constants satisfying all stated guarantees: exact answers, worst-case logarithmic query time, expected total update time \(O(u\log(M+2))\) for every oblivious finite sequence, and \(O((n+1)\log^c(n+2))\) space on every execution. Alternatively prove in Lean that no such representation and constants exist in the specified model. An insertion-only structure, approximate answers or a time bound retaining an unbounded extra logarithmic factor does not meet the full target.
